pages.name: Overview
pages.html:
Spacer is a science-fiction roleplaying game that focuses on travelling and exploring the galaxy. Spacer is designed to be setting neutral, although much of it is inspired by pulp science fiction.

Spacer stands for Science-fiction Procedural Adventure Conflict Exploration Roleplaying.

What is Spacer?

  • Spacer is a roleplaying game: In Spacer, a referee narrates the events of the game as they unfold, while the players are characters who navigate the narrative.
  • Spacer is a toolbox: Spacer is a toolbox to help referees build their own science-fiction campaign for a group of players or for solitaire play.
  • Spacer is a suggestion: All of the rules offered are suggestions. The referee is encouraged to change any rule to best suit their needs for their sci-fi campaigns.

What is Spacer not?

  • Spacer isn’t a campaign setting: There is no set-in-stone Spacer setting that the referee is expected to follow. The setting is implied by mechanics and terminology but is easy to change or modify to suit different sci-fi scenarios. While many different science-fiction game settings are defined to a known setting, Spacer is intended to be as neutral as possible for the referee to elaborate on.
  • Spacer isn’t complete: Spacer provides the framework for a referee to elaborate on. Due to the vast range of science fiction, it would be impossible to provide everything within one ruleset. Referees are encouraged to expand the scope of what is provided here to build additional systems using the provided mechanical framework to suit their needs, if necessary.
  • Spacer doesn’t have experience points: Most roleplaying games offer an automatic progression system by awarding experience points or some other currency that charts the advancement of a character. Spacer does not offer this, and instead requires characters to invest time and money into education to advance their characteristics or Skills.

The “Implied Setting”

In Spacer, the game focuses on the day-to-day life of an interstellar gig-worker paying off debts and trying to get by on their own terms. This means Spacer is less focused on heroics and instead prioritizes the mundane slice-of-life of living in humanity's far future as an average person. Spacer assumes a late-stage capitalist setting where larger interstellar governments are decentralized and as such, a social hierarchy has emerged headed by nobility, bureaucrats, oligarchs, and others who may be more immune to societal woes than most people. All planets will have their own unique legal systems which the spacer may need to navigate just to finish a job.

  • Spacing: Spacing is used to describe the lifestyle of space travellers known as spacers, who primarily work between planets and star systems, finding odd-jobs and adventure. Spacing provides the economic backbone of a decentralized interstellar civilization, bringing resources, people, and news from settled planets to frontier colonies.
  • Spacers: Spacers are interstellar travellers who seek odd-jobs and adventure as freelancing individuals. This can range from hauling freight between star systems or researching uninhabited planets to less savory jobs such as bounty-hunting, smuggling, or mercenary work.
  • Humans: Spacer focuses on human-dominated sectors of space, so assume humans are in charge of most power structures. Non-human intelligence may exist if the referee allows it.
  • Sophonts: Sophonts are biological non-human intelligent entities that have equivalent or advanced intelligence compared to humans and thus are also capable of interstellar travel. The referee is encouraged to create their own sophonts as needed for their campaign.
  • Psionics: Psionics is the power of the mind and its application to alter physical or perceived reality. Spacer assumes that psionics are real but are rare due to the general fear or distrust of psionic-using individuals.
  • Social Privilege: The social hierarchy of Spacer’s setting can be used as a basis to measure an individual's privilege in society. Some characters may have a noble title (see Social Standing pg.12), but that can easily be redefined as them being a bureaucrat, celebrity, or some other variety of person who may be more immune to societal woes than others.
  • Interstellar Travelling: Interstellar travel, measured in parsecs, always takes one week in “jump-space” via travelling at faster-than-light speeds. Each starship will be able to travel a number of parsecs per week as determined by their “jump drive.”
  • Jump-Space: An extra-dimensional form of travelling in which a spaceship slips between space-time in a pocket bubble to travel FTL.
  • Intrastellar Travel: Travelling between planets within the same star system will also still take time, between hours to days of travel, as determined by the starship's maneuver drive. “Jumping” cannot be used intrasystem due to the gravitational effects of the planets and sun(s).
  • Communication: News, information, and personal communications only travel as fast as a ship. Thus communication is not instantaneous but may take weeks or months to reach a location in the galaxy.

Book p.10

pages.name: Gameplay Expectations
pages.html:
The Primary Rule: Spacer is designed to be played mostly with dialog, with the referee explaining a situation and the players responding to the provided information. It is possible to have some sessions happen without making dice rolls. Spacer assumes a framework of roleplaying in which players using their characters’ intuition and situational plausibility to solve problems is considered more important than rolling dice to solve problems.

  • The Referee: Provides honest and clear information when describing what the players’ characters are experiencing. The referee should never be deceitful or cruel in any way but only function as the narrator of the events driven by the players’ characters. It is the responsibility of the referee to dictate the odds of success/failure or the consequences thereof to the players before a player commits their character to an action. Referees can provide increased or decreased chances of character success based on the amount of time being dedicated to an action and any other use of resources to aid an outcome.
  • The Characters: The players control characters in the game, typically referred to as spacers, but both spacer and character are interchangeable. Characters have agency in their decision-making and goal-setting. Characters only roll dice when needed, per the request of the referee, to help resolve any actions that may have meaningful or detrimental consequences. The focus of the player is to exist in the headspace of their character and react to the world being described by the referee.

The rest of the rules presented in Spacer are to be used AS NEEDED and function as suggestions for the referee and players to make informed decisions during roleplaying. Roleplaying is the primary focus; dice-rolling is secondary. The rest of the book provides the mechanical structure for roleplaying with dice rolls as needed to help inform gameplay and provide meaningful results to player decisions.

Book p.12

pages.name: Terminology
pages.html:
The following are terms used throughout this book.

Dice

1D: Represents one six-sided die.

2D: 2D represents two six-sided dice. Any number listed before D indicates how many six-sided dice are thrown. For example, 3D represents three six-sided dice.

D3: Represents a three-sided die. A result of a D3 can be accomplished using a normal 1D:

  • 1-2 results are a 1.
  • 3-4 results are a 2.
  • 5-6 results are a 3.

D66: This is when two dice are rolled, with the first die representing the tens place and the second die representing the ones place. Example: If you roll two dice and the result is 2 and 5, then the D66 result is 25.

D36: This is similar to the D66 but the first die rolled is a D3 instead of 1D.

Dice Modifier (DM): Dice Modifiers are numbers applied to rolled dice and are annotated as DM.

Effect: This is the difference between the difficulty of the roll and the final dice result. For example: if the player rolls a 10 against an average (8+) difficulty then the effect is +2. However, if they rolled a 6, then the effect is -2.

Characteristics

Characteristics: All characters will have the following characteristics which may change over the course of character creation and play-driven activities during the campaign.

  • Strength (STR): The level of physical strength a character has.
  • Dexterity (DEX): This represents a character's coordination, agility, and mobility.
  • Endurance (END): This represents the stamina and ruggedness of a character.
  • Intelligence (INT): This represents the level of reason and understanding a character has.
  • Education (EDU): This represents the level of education a character has. It can also be seen as their ability to learn and retain information.
  • Social Standing (SOC): This represents the level of societal privilege you have, typically due to your family and/or your connections within your culture. Anyone with a 10+ will have a noble title. This characteristic is flexible and may change with roleplaying, as determined by the referee.

Measurements

Measurements: All units of measurements will be metric.

  • G is grams.
  • Kg is kilogram, or one thousand grams.
  • T is a metric ton, or one thousand kilograms.
  • M is metres.
  • Km is kilometres.
  • Mm is megametres, or one million metres.
  • Gm is gigametres, or one billion metres.

Skills

Skills: Skills represent expertise or proficiency in a specific task. Knowing a skill will have a number rank, which is a +DM to a dice roll. Being untrained in a skill incurs -3DM.

Hexadecimal Notation

Hexadecimal Notation: Spacer uses hexadecimals to list information, to help streamline stats, information, and other important data, to aid with bookkeeping and referencing. Hexadecimal notation lists numbers 0-9 as they are written, but numbers 10-16 are assigned a letter.

Universal Personality Code (UPC): This is the hexadecimal code used to represent the characteristics of a spacer. Each digit of the code represents Strength, Dexterity, Endurance, Intelligence, Education, and Social Standing, in order.

  • Example: 698A76 - Strength 6, Dexterity 9, Endurance 8, Intelligence 10, Education 7, Social Level 6

Universal World Code (UWC): Similar to the UPC but used to describe a world’s features. Each code is elaborated on more in the World Creation section, pg. 90.

  • Example: Gagarin-3: BA6A743-9 N RI WA A - World Name (Gagarin-3), Hex Location (0101), Starport (B), Size (A), Atmosphere (6), Water Amount (A), Population (7), Government type (4), Law level (3), Tech level (9), Naval Base (N), Trade Codes (RI and WA), and Travel Zone (A for Amber Zone)

Credits

Credits (Cr): This is the term used for currency in Spacer. 1cr means one credit. For higher amounts, Kcr represents thousands of credits and Mcr represents millions of credits.

Tech Level

Tech Level (TL): This is a measurement of how advanced a piece of technology is. It can be applied to a planet’s local manufacturing and repair capabilities or as a mechanical framework the referee can use to determine the availability of certain tech.
